edge.title: The crowd with one way out
edge.setup: It is Deepavali week and the pandal or dandiya ground is packed. You came in through one gate and have not looked for another. There is a temporary stage, barricades and stalls, and people are still streaming in behind you. The good view is deep in the middle, the exit is somewhere behind a few thousand people.
edge.tell: If you cannot point to two exits without crossing the thickest part of the crowd, you are standing in a bottleneck.
move: On arrival, spend one minute locating two exits and note which side of the ground they are on; stay on that side, not in the centre.
Keep children and older family members at the edge, and agree a meeting point outside the gate in case you are separated.
If the crowd starts to compress, do not push against it: keep your feet moving with the flow, arms up near your chest, and angle sideways toward an edge.
Stay clear of makeshift stages, scaffolding and temporary stands, and leave before the closing rush rather than in it.
edge.why: Crowd disasters rarely need a big trigger. A rumour, a loud noise or a small structural failure becomes deadly only where density is high and people cannot disperse. You cannot control the trigger; you can control where you stand and how fast you can leave. Choosing position before anything goes wrong is the whole defence.
edge.variants: Same shape: cricket stadium gates after a match, concert and rally grounds, temple queues on festival days, railway foot-over-bridges at peak hour.

lens.name: Induced demand
lens.one_line: Adding road capacity creates new trips that fill it, so congestion returns at a higher throughput.
lens.detail: People who had given up on a route — shifted their timing, taken transit, moved closer — return once it gets easier. The new lane doesn't serve the old traffic; it reveals suppressed demand that was always there. Measured honestly, travel time often lands back where it started within a few years, now with more vehicles.
elsewhere: Build more parking and more people drive in.
Add engineers to a late project and the scope expands to absorb them.
Widen a hospital's OPD and the waiting room refills.
lens.test: When someone promises more capacity will fix congestion, ask: what was suppressed, and what happens when it comes back?
lens.today: Work has begun on the Mehkri Circle elevated corridor (New Indian Express), and BDA says Hebbal flyover and Ballari Road will stay open through 18 months of corridor work (The Hindu). I only have the headlines, not the traffic projections, but the model applies: a faster corridor tends to draw back the trips people had avoided, so do not plan your life around the promised saving. Plan around the disruption, which is certain, and treat the benefit as unproven.

moved.so_what: Expect slow lanes and diversions rather than a shutdown, so do not rearrange your route for good; check the day's status before leaving on that stretch.
